main_ideas:1.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the *main idea* — the single claim the entire passage is built to deliver. It is not asking which detail in the passage is true; it is asking which sentence captures the argument that every sentence is bending toward.
main_ideas:1.passage_breakdown:
Defoe's text is a single sustained contrast between two ways of preserving a message. First half: "The sermon is a sound of words spoken to the ear, and prepared only for present meditation and extends no farther than the strength of memory can convey it." That sets up speech as fleeting — its lifespan is the listener's memory.

Second half: "a book printed is a record, remaining in every man's possession, always ready to renew its acquaintance with his memory, and always ready to be produced as an authority or voucher to any reports he makes out of it, and conveys its contents for ages to come, to the eternity of mortal time, when the author is forgotten in his grave." Every clause here piles up the durability of print: it stays on the shelf, it can be re-read, it can be cited, it survives the author's lifetime.
main_ideas:1.reasoning: Both halves of the passage exist solely to set up one comparison: spoken word lasts only as long as memory; printed word lasts "for ages to come, to the eternity of mortal time." The main idea has to be exactly that contrast — print outlives speech in terms of permanence. Notice how the strongest language in the passage ("eternity of mortal time," "when the author is forgotten in his grave") is reserved for print's longevity, which signals where the author's argumentative weight is going.
main_ideas:1.distractors:
The option that says spoken messages are remembered better than printed ones reverses the comparison the passage actually makes — Defoe explicitly says speech "extends no farther than the strength of memory."

The option about a confident orator focuses on *delivery style* of speech, which the passage never discusses; it only discusses the medium, not the speaker's skill.

The option about authors being forgotten in their lifetimes pulls one phrase ("when the author is forgotten in his grave") out of context and turns it into the central claim — but in the passage that phrase is a *concession* used to dramatize how books outlive their writers, not to make a point about authorial fame.
main_ideas:1.takeaway: When the entire passage is built on a single contrast, the main idea must restate that contrast — not a supporting clause within it.

main_ideas:2.prompt_focus: This is a Main Ideas prompt for a passage that talks about a single novel but does so as evidence for a general claim about the whole series. The correct main idea must scale up to that general claim, not stay confined to the one novel mentioned.
main_ideas:2.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 introduces The Far Side of the World as one novel in O'Brian's twenty-book Aubrey/Maturin series.

Sentence 2 names a structural quirk of the novel: it has "a rather abrupt ending," but the next book "picks up neatly where The Far Side of the World leaves off." That is not a complaint — it is a setup for the larger argument.

Sentence 3 delivers that argument: "Thus, the sudden ending is only an issue if one considers the books as independent texts — the Aubrey/Maturin series is best thought of as a single incredibly long work, similar to other multivolume stories."
main_ideas:2.reasoning: The passage uses one specific novel's abrupt ending as an example, but the explicit thesis is about how the whole series should be read: as one continuous work rather than twenty separate books. Any choice that captures only the example (just two novels, just the ending) is too small. The correct main idea has to generalise from the example to the series as a whole, which is exactly what the word "thus" in the passage does.
main_ideas:2.distractors:
An option about the series being unfairly compared to The Forsyte Saga reverses the role of that comparison — in the passage The Forsyte Saga is offered as a flattering analogue, not as something the Aubrey/Maturin series is unfairly held against.

An option that calls two specific novels especially complex narrows the claim to those two books and introduces a complexity ranking the passage never makes.

An option about reader enjoyment despite flaws shifts the topic from structural argument to reader reception, which the passage never discusses.
main_ideas:2.takeaway: When a passage uses the word "thus" or "therefore," the main idea is almost always the conclusion that follows it, not the example that came before it.

main_ideas:3.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a passage that explicitly presents two opposing critical views. The correct option must capture the disagreement itself — not pick a side.
main_ideas:3.passage_breakdown:
The passage opens by introducing Master and Commander as part of the Aubrey/Maturin series.

It then sets up a debate: "Some critics have found fault with the abrupt endings of Master and Commander and other books in the series, saying that they do not finish conclusively but arbitrarily stop." That is view #1 — the structures are flawed.

The next sentence pivots: "Other critics, however, argue that the books should not be thought of as discrete texts with traditional beginnings and endings but as a single incredibly long work." That is view #2 — the structures are not flawed; they only seem flawed if you misread the form.

The passage stops there. It does not endorse either side.
main_ideas:3.reasoning: When a passage's structure is "some say X, but others say Y," the main idea is the existence of the disagreement, not either side's verdict. The correct interpretation must say that critics hold differing views about whether the structures of these novels are effective. Anything stronger — picking either side, or claiming one side is right — goes beyond what the passage actually establishes.
main_ideas:3.distractors:
An option claiming the structure makes Master and Commander especially intricate adopts only one critical view (the favourable side) and turns it into a fact, ignoring the dissenting view.

An option saying critics want the series to imitate The Forsyte Saga distorts the Forsyte Saga reference: in the passage, Forsyte Saga is offered as an analogue by the *favourable* camp, not as a model some critics want the series to copy and others reject.

An option about readers enjoying the books despite flaws conflates critical opinion with reader enjoyment — but the passage is about a *critical disagreement*, not about reader response.
main_ideas:3.takeaway: If the passage explicitly stages a debate between two camps, the main idea names the debate, not the winner.

main_ideas:4.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the central claim of a science passage that opens with background context and then introduces an experiment. The correct main idea has to capture the experiment's *finding*, not the setup.
main_ideas:4.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 names the baseline: horses and barn owls have 3D vision, which helps with depth perception.

Sentence 2 names the assumption being challenged: "Octopuses and squid are thought to lack 3D vision. Many researchers once thought the same about cuttlefish."

Sentence 3 introduces the test: Wardell's team "wanted to test whether this assumption was true."

The remaining sentences describe the test (cuttlefish in 3D glasses watching projected shrimp) and report that the cuttlefish reacted, which only matters if the cuttlefish actually perceived 3D.
main_ideas:4.reasoning: Every sentence after the first is doing one job — overturning the prior assumption about cuttlefish vision. The main idea must therefore be the contradiction of that assumption: contrary to what researchers had thought, cuttlefish may actually be able to see in 3D. This is a textbook "contrary to X, the new evidence shows Y" structure, and the main idea must be Y.
main_ideas:4.distractors:
An option about horses and barn owls' 3D vision restates a piece of background context ("long known") rather than the *new* claim the passage actually advances.

An option about cuttlefish being structurally similar to octopuses and squid invents a comparison the passage never makes; the passage compares 3D-vision *assumptions*, not anatomy.

An option that 3D vision allows animals to interact with one another generalises wildly; the passage is about distance/depth perception and never mentions animal-to-animal interaction.
main_ideas:4.takeaway: In a passage built on "researchers used to think X — but now we tested it," the main idea is the new finding, not the old assumption.

main_ideas:5.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a passage that contrasts an existing pair of studies with a newer study that combines both. The main idea must capture the relationship among the three studies.
main_ideas:5.passage_breakdown:
First, Protas and colleagues are introduced: they explored convergent evolution through *shared* genetic mechanisms.

Next, Zwaan and colleagues are introduced: they investigated convergence through *different* genetic mechanisms — but the passage flags a gap: "the relative prevalence of convergence through shared and different genetic processes is still poorly understood."

Finally Green and Extavour are introduced as the response to that gap: "This motivated…[them]…to evaluate both types of convergence in a single study."
main_ideas:5.reasoning: The whole passage is built around the word "both." Protas covered one mechanism. Zwaan covered the other. Green and Extavour cover both at once. The main idea is therefore that Green and Extavour's study addresses convergent evolution more comprehensively than either of the prior studies. The motivating phrase "This motivated" is the giveaway: the new study exists *because* the older two were each incomplete.
main_ideas:5.distractors:
An option claiming that, before Green and Extavour, convergent evolution was assumed to require shared mechanisms misreads the passage — Zwaan's existing work on different mechanisms shows that this assumption was not in place.

An option saying Green and Extavour relied on the data from Protas and Zwaan invents a methodological claim the passage never makes; the passage describes them "evaluat[ing] both types of convergence," not reusing earlier datasets.

An option that says both Protas and Green/Extavour compared shared vs different mechanisms is wrong about Protas, who studied only the shared-mechanism side.
main_ideas:5.takeaway: When a passage names earlier studies that each handled one piece of a problem, and a newer study that handles all the pieces, the main idea is the comprehensiveness of the newer study.

main_ideas:6.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a brief literary character description. The main idea must summarise what the entire description is showing about the character.
main_ideas:6.passage_breakdown:
Every clause about Robert is paired and balanced. "Daring, without being rash" — courage, but tempered. "Prompt, but not thoughtless" — quick to act, but reflective. "Firm without being harsh" — disciplined, but not cruel. "Kind and devoted to the company he drilled" — trusted by his peers. "Won the respect of his superior officers" — recognised from above.

There is no negative trait, no caveat, no ironic undercut. The passage is a list of qualities a soldier ought to have, all attributed to Robert.
main_ideas:6.reasoning: When every detail in a passage points the same direction, the main idea is that direction in summary form. Robert has every trait the military values — daring without recklessness, firmness without cruelty, devotion to subordinates, respect from superiors. The main idea must therefore be that he is well-suited to his role in the military.
main_ideas:6.distractors:
An option saying Robert tries hard to gain his comrades' attention misreads "kind and devoted": the passage describes natural leadership, not effort spent fishing for attention.

An option that he helps comrades despite his superiors not appreciating it contradicts "won the respect of his superior officers" — the superiors do appreciate him.

An option that Robert has flaws and good qualities directly contradicts the passage, which never names a flaw.
main_ideas:6.takeaway: In a balanced character sketch where every trait is praised, the main idea is the overall positive judgement of the character.

main_ideas:7.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the central argument of a science passage that opens with a long-held belief and then offers counter-examples. The correct main idea has to be the *correction* of the belief.
main_ideas:7.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1: animals use objects as tools for grooming, finding food, and protection.

Sentence 2 names the long-held belief: "For a long time, people thought tool use was unique to primates."

Sentence 3 explicitly debunks that belief: "Octopuses and other animals, though, have busted the myth that tool use requires hands." The word "busted" tells you exactly which side the passage is on.

Sentences 4–5 stack examples: octopuses use seashell halves; greater vasa parrots use date pits to grind shells into calcium powder.
main_ideas:7.reasoning: The phrase "have busted the myth" is the topic sentence. Everything that follows is evidence that primates are not the only tool users. The main idea must therefore be exactly that contradiction of the long-held belief — that, contrary to what was assumed, primates aren't the only animals to use tools.
main_ideas:7.distractors:
An option calling octopuses uniquely skillful with different tools elevates one example into the main claim and ignores the parrots; the passage treats octopuses as one of several counter-examples.

An option that there are many myths about tool use that researchers are challenging generalises to "many myths" when the passage discusses exactly one ("the myth that tool use requires hands").

An option that animals find tool use difficult flatly contradicts the examples, which all describe successful tool use.
main_ideas:7.takeaway: When a passage explicitly calls something "a myth" and then "busts" it, the main idea is the busted claim's opposite.

main_ideas:8.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a first-person literary passage. The correct main idea has to describe the inner experience the passage is dramatizing — not pick out one external detail.
main_ideas:8.passage_breakdown:
The narrator describes walking slowly under spring leaves, "drinking in the air, fragrant with the odor of young buds and sap." The natural sensory detail comes first.

Then the mental shift: he becomes "forgetful of musty papers, of the offices, of my chief, my colleagues, my documents." He is not just outdoors; he has mentally left work behind.

And the next clause links to a positive mental image: "thinking of the good things that were sure to come to me" and (continuing) of his youth. The setting prompts both forward-looking optimism and backward-looking memory.
main_ideas:8.reasoning: The passage is a closed circuit: the natural surroundings act on his mind, his mind sheds work concerns, and his mind fills with hopeful future thoughts and memories of youth. The main idea must capture that double effect — escape from work *and* the rise of hopeful thoughts and youthful memories. Any reading that captures only one half (only the escape, only the memories) is incomplete.
main_ideas:8.distractors:
An option that he has decided to leave his job and is returning to his childhood home invents biography that the passage never gives — he is just on a walk, not migrating.

An option that he is strategising about how projects could advance his career contradicts the passage, which says he is *forgetful* of work.

An option that the smells distract him from pressing work issues frames the experience as a problem; the passage frames it as a positive escape, not an irresponsible distraction.
main_ideas:8.takeaway: In a passage where setting triggers a mental shift, the main idea must include both the cause (the setting) and the effect (the mental shift).

main_ideas:9.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a passage that opens with one writer and then explicitly broadens to a wider phenomenon. The main idea must capture the broader pattern.
main_ideas:9.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 introduces Tanya Tagaq: a Cambridge Bay Inuit writer/musician.

Sentence 2 says her work "combin[es] traditional Inuit stories with popular genres of literature, such as fantasy fiction."

Sentence 3 is the pivot: "But Tagaq is not the only Indigenous writer to blend traditional stories with popular literature."

Sentence 4 supplies a parallel example: Stephen Graham Jones, of the Blackfeet Nation, blending Blackfeet oral tradition with horror fiction in The Only Good Indians.
main_ideas:9.reasoning: The pivot "But Tagaq is not the only…" is the giveaway: Tagaq is the entry point, but the passage's real point is the wider pattern. The main idea must reflect that pattern — that several Indigenous writers are blending traditional stories with popular literature, with Tagaq and Jones offered as two examples of the practice.
main_ideas:9.distractors:
An option about non-Indigenous authors considering Indigenous readers' expectations addresses the wrong audience entirely; the passage is about Indigenous writers' practice, not about non-Indigenous writers' duties.

An option about increased book sales adds a sales claim the passage never makes.

An option that one writer is more successful than the other invents a comparative ranking the passage never sets up.
main_ideas:9.takeaway: A sentence beginning "X is not the only…" almost always signals that the passage's main idea is the wider pattern, not X by themselves.

main_ideas:10.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a passage that describes two distinct kinds of work by the same artist and then unifies them under one theme. The correct main idea must include both kinds of work.
main_ideas:10.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 introduces Villasana, a Mexican textile artist whose method (yarn applied to photographs) weaves "stories of triumph."

Sentence 2 names group #1: cultural icons who are people of color — example, her depiction of Prince.

Sentence 3 names group #2: ordinary people — example, a young girl on a sidewalk.

Sentence 4 unifies them: Villasana "sees both of these approaches as ways of depicting the power and interconnectedness of all people."
main_ideas:10.reasoning: The passage explicitly groups Villasana's work into two categories and explicitly says she uses both to depict "the power and interconnectedness of all people." The main idea must therefore say that her work focuses on recognising both famous and everyday people, with strength and connection as the unifying theme. Any reading that captures only one category — only Prince, or only the girl — misses the explicit "both" claim.
main_ideas:10.distractors:
An option saying the girl-on-sidewalk painting is more about connection than resilience invents a ranking that the passage never makes — it says the *whole body of work* shows power and connection, not that one painting weights one theme over the other.

An option about a career trajectory from famous to everyday subjects invents a chronology the passage never gives.

An option about scholarly attention to the Prince painting introduces a critical-reception claim the passage never makes.
main_ideas:10.takeaway: When a passage explicitly says an artist's two kinds of work serve one shared idea, the main idea has to name both kinds of work and the shared idea.

main_ideas:11.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a science passage that defines a process, lists effects, and ends with a forward-looking remark. The main idea has to capture where the passage's *argument* lands, not just what it defines.
main_ideas:11.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 defines horizontal gene transfer (HGT) as "the exchange of genetic material between organisms not in a parent-offspring relationship" and notes it is "common among prokaryotes."

Sentence 2 names a real-world consequence: HGT "can have the effect of increasing bacterial resistance to antibiotics."

Sentence 3 (the conclusion) is forward-looking: "as such, an understanding of how to prevent horizontal gene transfer might result in the mitigation of dangerous pathogens (organisms that cause disease)."
main_ideas:11.reasoning: The defining sentence is the last one. The phrase "as such, an understanding of … might result in the mitigation of dangerous pathogens" is the payoff — and a Main Ideas answer must align with the payoff. The main idea is therefore that studying HGT may yield findings with useful applications (specifically, fighting dangerous pathogens). The earlier sentences are scaffolding that earns the right to make that forward-looking claim.
main_ideas:11.distractors:
An option that a common perception of HGT is inaccurate invents a misconception that the passage never raises — the passage simply describes HGT and its potential applications.

An option that HGT is more common than was thought adds a comparison-over-time claim that the passage does not make; the passage just says it is "common among prokaryotes."

An option that new research casts doubt on earlier findings is unsupported — no earlier findings are named, much less doubted.
main_ideas:11.takeaway: When a passage's last sentence is a "this might lead to" payoff, the main idea is the payoff.

main_ideas:12.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main *topic*. "Topic" and "main idea" are close cousins, but "topic" emphasises what the passage is *about* — the subject under discussion.
main_ideas:12.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 reports Lönnstedt and colleagues' 2013 conclusion that ocean acidification has "a strong effect" on the behavior of Pomacentrus amboinensis.

Sentence 2 immediately undercuts that with a methodological detail: "Lönnstedt and colleagues' study relied on a mean sample size of only about 28 fish."

Sentence 3 introduces Clements and colleagues' 2022 review of conclusions about ocean acidification on fish behavior — implicitly examining studies like Lönnstedt's.
main_ideas:12.reasoning: Every sentence after the first is doing one job: pointing at the small sample size as a possible weakness of the Lönnstedt study, and then introducing a later review that scrutinizes such conclusions. The topic is therefore a possible shortcoming of the Lönnstedt study on Pomacentrus amboinensis.
main_ideas:12.distractors:
An option about a discovery regarding the *evolution* of the species is wrong — the passage discusses behavior, not evolution.

An option about a change in fish behavior reported in 2022 misreads the 2022 reference: that paper is a *review of others' conclusions*, not a new behavioural finding.

An option about a newly identified cause of ocean acidification flips the topic completely; the passage treats acidification as a known cause, not as something whose origins are being studied.
main_ideas:12.takeaway: If a passage names one study and then immediately starts pointing out a weakness in it, the topic is the weakness.

main_ideas:13.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a research-summary passage that names a study and reports two findings. The main idea has to capture both findings as related results of the *same* study.
main_ideas:13.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 sets up the study: "In a large community science effort, biologist Abbigail Merrill and colleagues collaborated with hundreds of students … for more than three years to study how butterfly color and time of day relate to butterfly behavior." The study's two variables of interest are color and time of day.

Sentence 2 reports two findings: "butterfly color might influence behavior more than butterfly size does" AND "butterflies were observed to feed more often in the morning than at any other time of day."
main_ideas:13.reasoning: The study deliberately examined the influence of *both* color and time of day on butterfly behavior, and it reported a finding for each. The main idea must combine those findings: a large study suggested that butterfly color and time of day might both influence behavior.
main_ideas:13.distractors:
An option that location matters more than color and time of day adds a third variable the passage never discusses.

An option that color matters less than time of day reverses the color finding ("color might influence behavior more than size does") into a comparison the passage never makes.

An option that frames the passage as primarily about the *value of community-science collaboration* in general drifts away from the study's actual findings to a meta-claim the passage doesn't endorse.
main_ideas:13.takeaway: When a study explicitly names two variables and reports a finding for each, the main idea covers both.

main_ideas:14.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a biographical passage that names one famous association and then lists less-famous achievements as counterweight. The main idea has to capture *both* sides of that framing.
main_ideas:14.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 establishes Nixon's most famous association: Watergate, "a convoluted tale of criminality and eroded ethics," with associates like Magruder and Woods.

Sentence 2 pivots: "But Nixon's legacy is complex." It then lists positive items — affirming tribal sovereignty, attempting health-care reform that arguably anticipated later policies.
main_ideas:14.reasoning: The word "But" is the structural hinge: Nixon is famous for one thing, but his legacy includes more. The main idea must mirror that framing — Nixon is commonly linked with an infamous historical event, but that event overshadows other notable achievements. Any reading that drops one half (only Watergate, only the achievements) collapses the contrast the passage is built on.
main_ideas:14.distractors:
An option that Nixon's reputation is *primarily due to his associates* misreads the passage — Watergate is presented as Nixon's own famous association, with Magruder and Woods as part of the cast, not as the primary cause of Nixon's fame.

An option that some Nixon policies influenced later administrations captures only the achievements half and ignores the Watergate framing.

An option focused on Magruder and Woods themselves misses the passage's actual subject (Nixon's legacy).
main_ideas:14.takeaway: When a passage uses the structure "X is most famous for Y, but…," the main idea must include both Y and the contrasting clause.

main_ideas:15.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a passage that introduces a concept ("loanword") with two parallel examples. The main idea has to capture the *shared* point both examples are illustrating.
main_ideas:15.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 defines a loanword: "a word that originated in one language and was later adopted by another," with "tomato" as the headline example.

Sentence 2 traces "tomato": Nahuatl tomatl → Spanish tomate → English tomato.

Sentences 3–4 add a second example with the same structure: "Maize" also has Indigenous origins and entered English through Spanish, originally Taíno mahís.
main_ideas:15.reasoning: Both "tomato" and "maize" share three properties: they're English words, they're loanwords, and they originally came from Indigenous languages. The main idea must capture exactly the property the two examples have in common — both English words are loanwords from Indigenous languages.
main_ideas:15.distractors:
An option claiming Spanish words with Indigenous origins first passed through English reverses the actual chain of transmission (Indigenous → Spanish → English).

An option that Spanish borrowed roughly equally from Nahuatl and Taíno makes a quantitative comparison the passage never supports.

An option about meaning shifts during borrowing introduces a semantic-change claim the passage never discusses.
main_ideas:15.takeaway: Two parallel examples in a Main Ideas passage almost always exist to illustrate the same general claim.

main_ideas:16.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of an argumentative passage that explicitly debunks a popular interpretation. The main idea must capture the debunking, not the popular interpretation.
main_ideas:16.passage_breakdown:
The passage opens describing Smith's invisible-hand metaphor as "famed" and treated as "a robust model."

The pivot is the word "putatively" and the line "Note 'putatively'" — a clear flag that the passage is about to question the metaphor's reputation.

It then says Smith deploys the metaphor "only once in his economic writings — to make a narrow point about … mercantilism — and it was largely ignored" until "some twentieth-century economists eager to secure an intellectual pedigree for their views elevated it to a fully-fledged paradigm."
main_ideas:16.reasoning: The argument is explicit: the metaphor's reputation is not earned by its role in Smith's actual writing but is the work of later economists who promoted it for their own purposes. The main idea has to be exactly that: the metaphor's reputation comes from later promotion, not from its importance in Smith's own work.
main_ideas:16.distractors:
An option that endorses the metaphor as a critique of mercantilism that was later misinterpreted as a model softens the passage's stance — the passage is sceptical of the metaphor's exalted status, not merely tracking misinterpretation.

An option that the metaphor is nevertheless a useful model contradicts the sceptical thrust of the passage.

An option that twentieth-century economists came to *realise* the metaphor's robustness inverts the passage, which says they *promoted* it for their own ends.
main_ideas:16.takeaway: When a passage flags a key word with "Note 'X'" and then explains why X is misleading, the main idea is the corrective story.

main_ideas:17.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a passage about a single painting that quickly broadens into a claim about a whole artistic movement. The main idea must scale to the movement.
main_ideas:17.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 describes McLendon's Moonlit St. Lucie — a single palm tree silhouetted against shimmering water and moonlit sky — as "typical of paintings by the Florida Highwaymen."

Sentence 2 makes the broader claim: the Highwaymen are "remarkable for anticipating and amplifying cultural perceptions of Florida that became pervasive in the public consciousness," and their paintings are identifiable by recurring imagery — "placid inland rivers, windswept palm trees" — that the Highwaymen "perpetually revisited."
main_ideas:17.reasoning: The passage's argument is causal: the Highwaymen's paintings spread certain images of Florida into the public imagination, and those images became widely associated with Florida partly because of the Highwaymen's own influence. The main idea must reflect that — representative images across many Highwaymen paintings came to be widely associated with Florida partly thanks to the Highwaymen's influence.
main_ideas:17.distractors:
An option that singles out Moonlit St. Lucie as more highly regarded than other Highwaymen paintings invents a comparison the passage doesn't make; the painting is described as *typical*, not exceptional.

An option that the Highwaymen's popularity waned after the 1960s adds a chronological decline the passage never discusses.

An option that McLendon's natural-iconography paintings are otherwise indistinguishable from his peers' but that this iconography differentiates him is internally contradictory and inverts the passage's claim that the iconography unites the Highwaymen.
main_ideas:17.takeaway: If a passage uses a single artwork as "typical" of a movement, the main idea is about the movement, not the artwork.

main_ideas:18.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a comic literary passage in which one character's story keeps shifting. The main idea must capture the recurring pattern in those shifting versions.
main_ideas:18.passage_breakdown:
Harris narrates a rough Channel crossing in which seasickness was epidemic. The first version: "he and the captain were the only two living souls on board who were not ill."

Second version: "Sometimes it was he and the second mate who were not ill."

Third version: "but it was generally he and one other man."

Fourth version: "If not he and another man, then it was he by himself."
main_ideas:18.reasoning: Every retelling drops a different person from the well-list, but Harris is the constant. The narrator is highlighting Harris's habit of changing the supporting cast while always keeping his own immune status intact. The main idea must capture both halves — the changing details *and* the unchanging boast about his own wellness.
main_ideas:18.distractors:
An option about how much time Harris spent with passengers vs. the captain misreads the passage; the point isn't social time but who was sick.

An option that Harris struggles to remember the trip contradicts the passage, in which Harris is confidently telling and re-telling the story.

An option about Harris worrying about *future* rough waters projects ahead; the passage is about his past anecdotes.
main_ideas:18.takeaway: When a passage shows a character giving multiple versions of a story, the main idea usually targets the thing that *doesn't* change between versions.

main_ideas:19.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a biographical passage that traces an architect's career through phases. The main idea must capture the *change* the passage emphasises.
main_ideas:19.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 frames the career: spanning the 1920s–80s, Barragán's career "evolved through distinct phases."

Sentence 2 supplies the cause and the effect of one such phase: after travelling to the U.S. and Europe in the early 1930s, Barragán "began incorporating principles derived from functionalism and modernism" in works like the El Arenal Parish Church, whose unadorned geometric forms contrast with his earlier historically inspired houses for Robles Leon.
main_ideas:19.reasoning: The passage explicitly links a *change* in Barragán's design vocabulary (toward functionalism and modernism) to a *cause* (his time abroad). The main idea must reflect that linkage — a notable shift in his design aesthetic reflects the influence of his time abroad.
main_ideas:19.distractors:
An option that both the church and the houses for Robles Leon are paragons of functionalist/modernist design contradicts the passage, which contrasts the two.

An option that the houses are more experimental than the church inverts the description (the church is what changes; the houses are the historically inspired baseline).

An option that Barragán later abandoned modernism reads beyond the passage, which only describes his early adoption of it.
main_ideas:19.takeaway: If the passage explicitly says a career "evolved" and then names a turning point, the main idea is about that turning point.

main_ideas:20.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a science passage built on a "like X… however, because…" cause-and-consequence structure. The main idea must include both halves.
main_ideas:20.passage_breakdown:
First half: like other Hawaiian-only birds, the Kaua'i 'amakihi has "adapted to life in a well-defined habitat, resulting in highly specialized physical and behavioral characteristics that aid the species in survival." That is the *helpful* side of specialisation.

Second half: "However, because the Kaua'i 'amakihi is highly specialized, it is especially vulnerable to environmental changes that can disrupt the delicately balanced ecosystem in which it lives." That is the *risky* side of the same specialisation.
main_ideas:20.reasoning: The two halves describe one trait — specialisation — and its two consequences (good for survival in stable conditions, bad in changing conditions). The main idea must capture both: the bird is unique to Hawaii, highly specialised, and therefore particularly susceptible to habitat disturbance.
main_ideas:20.distractors:
An option saying the bird is related to other Hawaiian birds but does not share their habitat is directly contradicted by "like many other bird species that live only on the Hawaiian archipelago."

An option that emphasises only the *similarity to other specialised Hawaiian birds* drops the vulnerability half of the passage.

An option that all Hawaiian birds can only live in unique Hawaiian habitats over-generalises from the specific case of the Kaua'i 'amakihi.
main_ideas:20.takeaway: In a "specialised but vulnerable" passage, the main idea always names both qualities and ties them together.

main_ideas:21.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a literary passage in which a character is alone, plays sad music, and is described in a particular setting. The main idea must explain the *connection* the passage is drawing between the character's actions and his inner state.
main_ideas:21.passage_breakdown:
The setting: Padre Florentino is in "his solitary retreat on the shore of the sea," with the sea extending out to the horizon through the open windows.

The action: he is "relieving the monotony by playing on his harmonium sad and melancholy tunes."

The implied state: "sad and melancholy tunes" played to relieve monotony tells us about his mood, not his repertoire — the music's emotional colour matches the player's.
main_ideas:21.reasoning: Solitude + sea + sad music chosen to "reliev[e] the monotony" is a compact emotional portrait. The main idea must tie those elements together by saying that the sadness of his music reflects his own feelings.
main_ideas:21.distractors:
An option about the residence's isolation seizes on a setting detail ("solitary retreat") and ignores the music and the man's feelings.

An option that he prefers playing music to listening to it adds a preference the passage never makes.

An option that he has dedicated himself to becoming a skilled musician invents an aspiration the passage doesn't suggest — he plays "to relieve the monotony," not to develop a craft.
main_ideas:21.takeaway: In a brief literary character sketch, music or other expressive activity that matches the surrounding mood usually IS the main idea — the activity expresses the inner state.

main_ideas:22.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a 19th-century essay-style passage that uses a metaphor to make a claim about a social role. The main idea must convert the metaphor into its underlying argument.
main_ideas:22.passage_breakdown:
Emerson calls scholars "the priests of that thought which establishes the foundations of the earth." The metaphor casts intellectuals as a kind of clergy — keepers of essential ideas.

The next clause widens the role: "No matter what is their special work or profession, they stand for the spiritual interest of the world."

The conclusion is the warning: "it is a common calamity if they neglect their post in a country where the material interest is so predominant as it is in America."
main_ideas:22.reasoning: Emerson's argument is that in a society dominated by material concerns, scholars are responsible for preserving ideas — and their abandonment of that role would be a public calamity. The main idea must therefore be exactly that: in a country where citizens are largely preoccupied with tangible gains, it is crucial that some people work to foster and preserve ideas.
main_ideas:22.distractors:
An option that military experience leads Americans to contemplate human life is unrelated to anything in the passage; the passage never discusses military experience.

An option that intellectuals are too concerned with material things flips the passage's stance — the passage warns about the surrounding country's materialism, not about scholars' personal materialism.

An option that descriptions of scholars unfairly diminish them shifts focus to *how scholars are characterised by others*, which is not what the passage discusses.
main_ideas:22.takeaway: When a metaphor opens a passage, the main idea must restate the metaphor's underlying claim, not the metaphor itself.

main_ideas:23.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a passage that praises a work and then identifies a specific limitation. The main idea must capture both the praise and the limitation.
main_ideas:23.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 describes The Fifty-Year Mission: "over a thousand pages across two volumes," billed as "the complete, uncensored, unauthorized oral history" of Star Trek.

Sentence 2 lays out the praise: "The work aspires to be comprehensive by, for example, including accounts from cast and crew members of every Star Trek television series and film to date."

Sentence 3 introduces the limitation: "But while The Fifty-Year Mission is clearly a unique and valuable resource, it has a shortcoming common among oral histories: it lacks a clear authorial point of view that could otherwise unite the various accounts into a cohesive whole."
main_ideas:23.reasoning: The passage is balanced: a worthwhile attempt at comprehensive Star Trek history, weakened by the absence of an authorial unifying viewpoint. The main idea must include both — the work is a worthwhile, ambitious effort with one important limitation built into its approach.
main_ideas:23.distractors:
An option about TV vs. film coverage invents a quantitative comparison the passage doesn't make.

An option that the work *lacks information about many key events* misstates the limitation — the passage faults its lack of unifying viewpoint, not its coverage of events.

An option that focuses on people who *did not* participate inverts the passage, which says it includes accounts from "every" series and film.
main_ideas:23.takeaway: When a passage explicitly says "X is a unique and valuable resource, but it has a shortcoming," the main idea must contain *both* the value and the shortcoming.

main_ideas:24.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a science passage that opens with a question and then proposes an explanation. The main idea must capture the proposed explanation as a whole.
main_ideas:24.passage_breakdown:
The passage opens with a contrast question: "Why do black-footed cats purr but leopards roar?"

It then proposes the answer: this difference "may be partly due to a U-shaped bone in their throats called the hyoid."

It supplies the supporting evidence: black-footed cats have a *rigid* hyoid that rumbles → purr; leopards have a *flexible* hyoid attached by a stretchy ligament that black-footed cats lack → roar.
main_ideas:24.reasoning: The passage explicitly proposes hyoid-bone differences as a *partial* explanation of the purr-vs-roar contrast. The main idea must therefore tie the hyoid difference to the behavioral difference between the two species.
main_ideas:24.distractors:
An option that simply lists the structural difference (rigid vs. flexible hyoid) is true but missing the *explanatory* function — it doesn't tie the difference to purring vs. roaring.

An option that frames roaring purely as a hyoid+ligament feat narrows the answer to leopards and ignores the original question.

An option claiming researchers are uncertain why these cats differ contradicts the passage, which actually offers a hypothesis.
main_ideas:24.takeaway: When a passage opens "why does X happen?" and offers a hypothesis, the main idea is the hypothesis.

main_ideas:25.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a passage that links a research finding to a theoretical model. The main idea must identify the *relationship* between the finding and the model.
main_ideas:25.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 reports the empirical finding: van Berlo et al.'s meta-analysis confirms that advergames "can elicit player interest" but "may not facilitate subsequent recall of product and brand information."

Sentence 2 introduces the theoretical lens: "This phenomenon can be explained by the finite nature of cognitive capacity as it is articulated in Annie Lang's limited capacity model of motivated mediated message processing."

Sentence 3 applies that model to the finding: cognitive resources go to gameplay mechanics, leaving "little or no capacity for encoding and storing" the brand info.
main_ideas:25.reasoning: The passage's argument is one-directional: van Berlo et al.'s finding is the explanandum (thing to be explained); Lang's limited-capacity model is the explanans (the explanation). The main idea must capture exactly that relationship — Lang's model provides the means of explaining van Berlo's recall finding.
main_ideas:25.distractors:
An option about purchase behaviour misreads van Berlo's finding (it concerns *recall*, not purchasing).

An option that Lang's model says advergames can succeed if they balance mechanics and brand contradicts the passage's clear claim that mechanics consume the cognitive budget.

An option that frames van Berlo as *corroborating* a Lang conclusion gets the order backwards: the passage uses Lang to explain van Berlo, not van Berlo to verify Lang.
main_ideas:25.takeaway: When one source's finding is explained using another source's model, the main idea names the explanans-explanandum relationship — not just one half.

main_ideas:26.prompt_focus: Same template as Q20: a "like other specialised birds … however, because specialised, vulnerable" passage. The main idea must combine specialisation with vulnerability.
main_ideas:26.passage_breakdown:
First clause: like other Hawaiian-only birds, the 'akeke'e has "adapted to life in a well-defined habitat, resulting in highly specialized physical and behavioral characteristics that aid the species in survival."

Second clause: "However, because the 'akeke'e is highly specialized, it is especially vulnerable to environmental changes that can disrupt the delicately balanced ecosystem in which it lives."
main_ideas:26.reasoning: Identical structure to Q20: the same trait (specialisation) is presented as both an adaptation and a liability. The main idea must therefore say that the 'akeke'e is unique to Hawaii, highly specialised, and therefore particularly susceptible to habitat disturbance.
main_ideas:26.distractors:
An option that all Hawaiian birds can only live in unique Hawaiian habitats over-generalises from the single species under discussion.

An option that emphasises only the bird's relationships to other species drops the vulnerability half and replaces it with a phylogenetic claim the passage doesn't make.

An option that the bird is unrelated to other Hawaiian species contradicts the explicit "like many other bird species" framing.
main_ideas:26.takeaway: Recurring template — when the passage says "specialised → vulnerable," the main idea must name both.

main_ideas:27.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a passage about a research methodology and what it offers. The main idea must capture the *combined* benefits the passage names.
main_ideas:27.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 defines community science: "professional scientists collaborating with members of the public to study a topic."

Sentence 2 names benefit #1: it "can promote community engagement by offering insight into the daily life of a scientist."

Sentence 3 names benefit #2: it "greatly increases the amount of data that can be collected," with the Herzel butterfly study as an example.
main_ideas:27.reasoning: The passage explicitly lists two distinct benefits of community science. The main idea must combine them — community science increases public understanding of scientists' work *and* generates large amounts of data, benefiting communities and researchers alike.
main_ideas:27.distractors:
An option naming a different researcher (Abbigail Merrill) and claiming surprise at the public-engagement effect attaches the wrong story to the passage.

An option that the approach is *less likely* to help researchers obtain accurate data flatly contradicts the data benefit.

An option that significantly increases data collection but doesn't affect public understanding drops benefit #1, which the passage explicitly names.
main_ideas:27.takeaway: If a passage names two distinct benefits of a method, the main idea must include both.

main_ideas:28.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main *topic* of a passage that introduces a scenario and unpacks its implications. The main idea must name the scenario the passage is *about*.
main_ideas:28.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1: "Sometimes an animal will encounter another member of its own species that it doesn't have any connection with. (For example, African lions that aren't in the same pride might meet.)"

Sentence 2 lists decisions the animals must then make: compete for a mate, help in a fight against a predator, or some other outcome.

Sentence 3 frames it: "the animals have to think carefully about possible risks and benefits."
main_ideas:28.reasoning: Every detail in the passage is anchored to one type of event: an encounter between unrelated members of the same species. The main topic is therefore precisely "a kind of meeting between animals of the same species."
main_ideas:28.distractors: Topics about predators, near-extinct species, or different environments are background frames the passage never makes its subject. The passage isn't about predators; it's about same-species meetings, and a fight against a predator is mentioned only as one of the *decisions* in such a meeting.
main_ideas:28.takeaway: Every example in the passage points to the same scenario — that scenario is the topic.

main_ideas:29.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a Defoe passage almost identical to Q1. Same comparison; same main-idea answer.
main_ideas:29.passage_breakdown:
First half: "The sermon is a sound of words spoken to the ear, and prepared only for present meditation, and extends no farther than the strength of memory can convey it."

Second half: "a book printed is a record, remaining in every man's possession, always ready to renew its acquaintances with his memory, and always ready to be produced as an" authority — exactly as in Q1.
main_ideas:29.reasoning: Identical reasoning to Q1. The whole passage is one sustained contrast: spoken words vanish with memory; printed words persist beyond the author. The main idea must be the durability of print over speech.
main_ideas:29.distractors:
Reversing the comparison so spoken messages outlast printed ones contradicts the passage.

Saying that spoken messages from non-experts can be ignored is a value judgment the passage doesn't make.

Saying that authors are forgotten in their lifetimes lifts a phrase out of context.
main_ideas:29.takeaway: Recurring stem — the print-vs-speech contrast always centres on permanence.

main_ideas:30.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a research-data passage that reports a comparison and then *explicitly rules out* one explanation. The main idea must include both the comparison and the ruled-out explanation.
main_ideas:30.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 sets up Moran/Rodriguez's study: 618 Quito respondents and 683 Buenos Aires respondents surveyed about parks.

Sentence 2 reports the headline finding: 82.9% of Quito respondents use city parks vs. 69.9% of Buenos Aires respondents. Quito > Buenos Aires.

Sentence 3 takes the obvious explanation off the table: Quito respondents reported *much lower* access to other desired amenities near parks, so "the difference in park use can't be explained by Quito residents having more access to desired nonpark amenities near parks."
main_ideas:30.reasoning: The passage does two things at once: announces the gap and pre-empts a tempting explanation for it. The main idea has to do both — the gap exists, but it isn't due to greater access to nearby amenities in Quito.
main_ideas:30.distractors:
An option that the gap is partly due to a greater prevalence of parks in Quito invents a different explanation the passage never offers.

An option about more amenities increasing park use in only one city contradicts the passage's general claim that amenities don't explain the gap.

An option that Buenos Aires has parks closer to amenities but Quito has more amenities overall reverses the structure of the passage's data.
main_ideas:30.takeaway: If a passage reports a finding and then *explicitly rules out* an explanation, the main idea must include the ruled-out explanation.

main_ideas:31.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a literary-passage opening in which the narrator reflects on her life as she enters a new apartment. The main idea must connect that reflection to *this* moment.
main_ideas:31.passage_breakdown:
Setup (provided in the prompt's framing): the narrator has just rented an apartment and is entering it for the first time.

Her reflection: "Over the years there have been many times when my destiny has delivered me unexpected moments, unforeseen twists and turns that I've had to handle on the fly as they appeared. Occasionally I was ready for them; very often I wasn't."
main_ideas:31.reasoning: Why is she reflecting on past life-changing turning points right at this moment? Because *this moment* — stepping into the new apartment — is one of those turning points. The reflection is a frame for recognising that the present moment marks a major shift in her life. The main idea must capture that self-awareness.
main_ideas:31.distractors:
An option about future business success invents a goal the passage doesn't mention.

An option that she has always had a plan for big moments contradicts "very often I wasn't [ready]."

An option about gratitude to others invents a sentiment that the passage doesn't express.
main_ideas:31.takeaway: When a literary opening has a character reflect on life's turning points, the main idea is usually that the *present* moment is one of those turning points.

main_ideas:32.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a passage that names a controversial decision and then reports its outcome. The main idea must include both the controversy and the outcome.
main_ideas:32.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 establishes the decision: Ngugi wa Thiong'o, who had previously published in English, began writing in Gikuyu in the 1970s, and "several fellow writers and critics cautioned that doing so might make his works inaccessible outside his own community."

Sentence 2 names a more pragmatic alternative: Kiswahili "would be a more practical choice."

Sentence 3 reports the outcome: "Rejecting their arguments, Ngugi went on to author dozens of acclaimed works in Gikuyu that have been translated into a total of more than thirty languages."
main_ideas:32.reasoning: The structure is "critics warned X; the writer ignored them; success followed." The main idea must join those parts: the decision was met with scepticism, but it didn't prevent him from achieving literary success.
main_ideas:32.distractors:
An option that focuses *only* on the translation outcome drops the scepticism part of the story.

An option about literary experts believing fame requires widely understood languages reverses what the experts said in the passage (they recommended Kiswahili for accessibility, not abandoning Gikuyu for fame).

An option that turns the passage into a manifesto about authors' duty to use native languages reads Ngugi's personal decision as a general doctrine the passage doesn't explicitly endorse.
main_ideas:32.takeaway: When a passage stages "sceptics warned X, the protagonist did X anyway, and succeeded," the main idea names both the warning and the success.

main_ideas:33.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a literary passage in which the narrator observes a transition from city to countryside on a boat. The main idea must connect the geographical transition to the river itself.
main_ideas:33.passage_breakdown:
The narrator stands at the bow of the boat "looking at the quays, the trees, the houses and the bridges disappearing behind us." The cityscape recedes.

Then a structural marker appears: "And suddenly I perceived the great viaduct of Point du Jour which blocked the" — the viaduct functions as the threshold between Paris and the countryside, and the river itself changes character on the other side.
main_ideas:33.reasoning: The passage aligns the urban-to-rural transition with the river's own transformation: the viaduct marks where Paris ends and the country begins, and the Seine itself shifts in step. The main idea must therefore say that the narrator perceives a parallel between the shift from urban to rural environment and the changes in the river.
main_ideas:33.distractors:
An option that the narrator is anxious for the trip to be over contradicts the calm, observational tone of the passage.

An option about being *surprised* and *exhilarated* by an unknown place misreads the passage; the narrator is observing an expected transition, not exploring the unknown.

An option that contrasts apprehension with the river's tranquility introduces a feeling (apprehension) the passage never names.
main_ideas:33.takeaway: If a literary passage describes a setting changing in two registers at once (city → country, river → river), the main idea names that parallel.

main_ideas:34.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a longer Maupassant excerpt that explicitly describes how the Seine changes between Paris and the countryside. The main idea must capture the *contrast* between the two stretches of river.
main_ideas:34.passage_breakdown:
First, the cityscape recedes as the boat moves down the Seine.

Then the viaduct of Point du Jour "blocked the river. It was the end of Paris, the beginning of the country."

Beyond the viaduct, "behind the double row of arches the Seine, suddenly spreading out as though it had regained space and liberty, became all at once the peaceful river which flows through the plains, alongside the wooded hills, amid the meadows, along the edge of the forests."
main_ideas:34.reasoning: The passage explicitly says that *outside* Paris the Seine "spread[s] out" and becomes peaceful. The implicit comparison is with the river *inside* Paris, which was bounded by quays, bridges, and the viaduct itself. The main idea must therefore say that the Seine is more confined and rough in Paris than in the countryside.
main_ideas:34.distractors:
An option that the arches create a small area of heavy current narrows the passage to one localized feature instead of the global contrast.

An option that the Seine is similar to Paris in being beautiful and slow to change misreads the passage; the passage emphasises *change* in the river as the boat leaves the city.

An option about the water becoming clearer adds a colour-of-water claim the passage never makes.
main_ideas:34.takeaway: When a passage explicitly contrasts "in the city" vs. "in the country" via a single object (the river), the main idea is that contrast.

main_ideas:35.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a literary-criticism passage that describes a seeming paradox and then resolves it via a quoted poet. The main idea must capture the resolution.
main_ideas:35.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 sets up the surface paradox: "Although notorious for its strict formal requirements, the sonnet is nevertheless represented by such wide-ranging examples as Maggie Anderson's 'Sonnet for Her Labor' and Tyehimba Jess's 'Millie and Christine McCoy' — poems that differ remarkably in subject, rhythm, and structure."

Sentence 2 acknowledges the surface tension ("It may seem counterintuitive…") and then resolves it via Carl Phillips: "the form invites experimentation: when a genre's conventions are as recognizable as those of the sonnet, the opportunity to subvert them is especially irresistible."
main_ideas:35.reasoning: The argument is that the sonnet's perceived rigidity is exactly what *encourages* experimentation. The main idea must restate this: the sonnet encourages a surprising amount of variety, even though certain characteristics associated with it suggest this would be unlikely.
main_ideas:35.distractors:
An option that distinguishes Anderson and Jess as exceptions while "most modern examples are conventional" contradicts the passage's claim that the form itself invites variety.

An option about the form's continued popularity inverts the focus from variety to popularity.

An option that for a long time very little innovation occurred adds a chronological story the passage never tells.
main_ideas:35.takeaway: When a passage stages a paradox ("X seems Y but is actually Z"), the main idea is the resolution (Z), not the paradox.

main_ideas:36.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a science passage about an experiment with a counterintuitive premise. The main idea must capture the experiment's surprising conclusion.
main_ideas:36.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 frames the question: how does habitat navigation work in fish?

Sentences 2–3 describe the unusual setup: Givon's team taught goldfish to drive a motorised tank on *land*, with the tank programmed to move in the direction the fish swam.

Sentences 4–5 report the result: the fish were tasked with steering to a pink board, succeeded often, got treats. Givon's conclusion: "their navigational skills aren't specific to an aquatic environment."
main_ideas:36.reasoning: The whole passage exists to deliver one surprising conclusion: fish, with mechanical help, can navigate even on land. The main idea must restate that conclusion in plain terms.
main_ideas:36.distractors:
An option that fish can navigate *only* in their natural aquatic environment contradicts the result.

An option about treats motivating animals generalises to a different topic (training methods).

An option that an animal's navigational skills depend on its particular environment is exactly the claim the passage *refutes*.
main_ideas:36.takeaway: If a passage's whole structure is "experiment → surprising result," the main idea is the surprising result.

main_ideas:37.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of a brief biographical passage that uses one woman as an entry point to discuss a wider group. The main idea must scale to the wider group.
main_ideas:37.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 frames the topic: "Women like Dorothy T. Blum made important early contributions to the history of US cryptology."

Sentences 2–3 describe Blum specifically: 1940s Army cryptology; later joining the NSA; pioneering computer-based cryptoanalysis.

Sentence 4 explicitly extends the story: "Blum and others like her helped make it possible for more women — such as Maureen Baginski."
main_ideas:37.reasoning: The passage uses Blum as one example and Baginski as another to make a general claim about women's contributions to cryptology. The main idea must capture exactly that — women like Blum and Baginski have contributed to the field.
main_ideas:37.distractors:
An option that focuses on what cryptology is as a field reduces the main idea to a definition the passage offers only as background.

An option that says Blum and Baginski worked together on a project misreads the passage — Baginski is named as a *successor* enabled by Blum, not as a co-worker.

An option that cryptology should be taught more often in schools is a policy claim the passage never makes.
main_ideas:37.takeaway: Two named women + the framing "women like…" almost always makes the main idea a claim about women's contributions in general.

main_ideas:38.prompt_focus: The prompt asks for the main idea of an academic passage that situates one piece of research relative to its field and then names that research's distinctive contribution. The main idea must include both the field placement and the unique contribution.
main_ideas:38.passage_breakdown:
Sentence 1 describes the topic: Drelichman and Voth's research on Philip II's debt defaults, and notes it "relates to other work on European early modern state finance, including Hoffman and Norberg's research."

Sentence 2 names the unique contribution: "their reconstruction of the earliest extant set of annual fiscal records for any sovereign state, demonstrating in turn that Philip's defaults were caused by short-term cash shortages, not long-term unsustainable debts."
main_ideas:38.reasoning: The passage explicitly identifies two things: (1) Drelichman and Voth's place in the wider field, and (2) what makes their work distinctive — the new dataset and what it reveals about Philip II. The main idea must combine both: they advanced the field by assembling a novel collection of evidence that gave them insight into Philip II's debt defaults.
main_ideas:38.distractors:
An option that contrasts Drelichman/Voth with Hoffman/Norberg by claiming the latter contains no analysis of early sovereign-state records misreads the passage; Hoffman/Norberg are mentioned as related work, not as a foil.

An option that ruling Spain and Belgium caused short-term cash problems explains the *empirical finding* of the study but ignores the methodological achievement (the new dataset).

An option that Drelichman/Voth's work simply builds on Hoffman/Norberg with added nuance under-credits the unique reconstruction the passage explicitly highlights.
main_ideas:38.takeaway: When a passage names one researcher's *unique contribution* to a field, the main idea must mention both the field context and the contribution.
